paragraphs.text: It started with a trip to the Scientific Center here in Kuwait. After a leisurely stroll through the aquarium, my beloved mother took us to the gift shop. That was when I saw it: a shiny, black painted, majestically mounted Newtonian telescope.
I begged for it. I was barely ten and knew almost nothing about telescopes, but I begged anyway, and with some reluctance she obliged.

That very night I was on our rooftop, a fish out of water, utterly incompetent with this great instrument in front of me. Yet I persisted, and lo and behold, by a grand and perhaps divine miracle, the Moon came into focus. It was full, and I saw the scars ornamenting its surface. My breath was caught by the sight, the intense glow and the utter blackness surrounding it, and I had a feeling in my stomach that I now characterise as the feeling one gets when the course of their life is beginning to change.

Life, however, comes with many distractions and challenges. As my teenage years came prowling we moved to the UK, and my key to the universe lay in storage, collecting dust and bearing the weight of a young boy's regret. University came and went. Hills conquered and valleys endured, countless highs and multifarious lows. Then I came home twelve years later, laden with scars I cherished and wounds I abhorred.

I was a pharmacist now, employed and working, with some income I could spare on hobbies. My family had moved house while I was away studying, and when I came back to Kuwait someone had unearthed a grey plastic case that held a young boy's passion within, barely contained. I remember opening that case and being overtaken by the heartbreak. With misty eyes I took the old hunk of aluminium out of its tomb, dusted its mirrors and cleaned it whole. Then I made a decision.
I was to become an amateur astronomer.

I spent weeks researching the hobby, quickly familiarising myself with all things optical. I recalibrated my budget and bought my second telescope, a 12 inch Dobsonian I could barely move, and I took it to the desert the following night. It was there that I felt it again, deep within my essence, that same feeling from more than a decade ago, when I beheld the rings of Saturn for the first time in my life.

I am an emotional person, that I don't deny, and my fingers were literally trembling while I was changing eyepieces. I screamed at my sister to come and take a look, then pushed her away (gently, of course), pulled out my phone and took a picture. I posted it everywhere and people responded, but I kept failing to induce in them that same feeling I had felt, and failed to communicate my passion. The photo was terrible.
“There has to be a better way to do this,” I told my sister after we came home.

“Probably,” she replied, and went to shower off and sleep. I, on the other hand, spent all night on the internet trying to answer that question. Finally, at around 6am, I placed an order for my first ZWO planetary camera, and down the rabbit hole I was blissfully lost.
